Build a design specification from a fitted mixed model

Source: R/spec_from_model.R
spec_from_model.Rd

Read a design specification off a linear mixed model already fitted with lme4::lmer() or lmerTest::lmer(). The fixed effects, the random-effect standard deviations and correlations, and the residual standard deviation are taken from the fit, and the numbers of subjects and items may be raised at the same time, so that a pilot study or a published model becomes the starting point of a power analysis. The fixed effects of a pilot are its point estimates, and a study powered for them tends to be underpowered. A message names them on every call, and sesoi or effects = "safeguard" replaces them (see Details). Requires the lme4 package.

Usage

spec_from_model(
  fit,
  name = NULL,
  seed = 1,
  n_subject = NULL,
  n_item = NULL,
  family = NULL,
  round = NULL,
  effects = c("estimate", "safeguard"),
  safeguard_level = 0.6,
  sesoi = NULL,
  counterbalance = TRUE
)

Arguments

fit

A fitted linear mixed model, of class lmerMod (from lme4::lmer()) or lmerModLmerTest (from lmerTest::lmer()). Anything else is refused with a message saying what to pass instead.

name

A label for the returned specification. Defaults to "from_model".

seed

The master seed of the returned specification. Defaults to 1.

n_subject

Number of subjects for the returned specification. Defaults to the number of levels the fit actually had, and is normally raised above it, since scaling a pilot design up is the point of reading a specification off a pilot fit.

n_item

Number of items, treated the same way as n_subject. An error when the model has no second crossed grouping factor to act as items, because there is then no item unit to resize.

family

The response family of the returned specification. NULL, the default, gives "gaussian", which is what a lmer fit is on the scale it was fitted on. A single string names another family, and a list such as list(family = "shifted_lognormal", shift = 200) also supplies the parameters of that family which a Gaussian fit cannot provide.

round

Decimal places for the simulated response, passed through to response.round. NULL, the default, leaves the response unrounded.

effects

Where the coefficients of the returned specification come from. "estimate", the default, takes the fit's point estimates, as earlier versions did. "safeguard" takes the bound of each coefficient's two-sided safeguard_level interval nearer zero, and stops with an error when that interval includes zero (see Details). Either way, a coefficient named in sesoi takes the value given there, and the intercept is the fit's.

safeguard_level

The confidence level of the intervals behind effects = "safeguard", a single number greater than 0 and less than 1. The default of 0.6 follows Perugini, Gallucci and Costantini (2014).

sesoi

NULL, the default, or a named numeric vector that sets coefficients to a smallest effect size of interest on the scale of the fit, as in sesoi = c(cond = 0.03). The names are the returned specification's coefficient keys, which write an interaction as a:b, and a name that is not among them is refused.

counterbalance

Whether a factor that the pilot counterbalanced sets counterbalance in the returned specification, which then declares specification version 0.4 (see Details). TRUE, the default, plans the pilot's design, unless its subjects each saw only some of the items or its model has a term named list. FALSE returns a fully crossed specification that releases reading version 0.3 accept, with a warning that the power computed from it is too high.

Value

A design specification as a nested list, carrying the lowest spec_version that reads it, 0.4 when it sets counterbalance and 0.3 otherwise, and validated with validate_spec(), so it can be passed directly to simulate_design(), power_mixed() or spec_json(). Two attributes record the readings that the fit did not settle on its own: group_mapping, a named character vector giving the specification unit each of the fit's grouping factors became, and column_kinds, a named character vector giving each model-frame column the classification "factor" or "predictor". A third, effects, is a list recording where the coefficients came from. Its method is the value of effects, its level the safeguard_level applied, or NA with "estimate", and its sesoi the keys of the coefficients set from sesoi. All three are attributes rather than fields so that the specification itself stays within the portable schema.

Details

Settling on plausible random-effect standard deviations with nothing to read them from is the step that most often stops a simulation-based power analysis before it starts, and the tutorials on the method converge on the same remedy, which is to take the variance components from a pilot fit or from a published model (Green and MacLeod, 2016; Kumle et al., 2021; DeBruine and Barr, 2021). This function performs that transfer, and the specification it returns can be enlarged and passed straight to simulate_design() or power_mixed().

The fixed effects are another matter. They are the pilot's point estimates, which a small pilot measures imprecisely, and a pilot followed up because its effect looked promising has on average overestimated that effect. A study powered for such an estimate therefore tends to have less power than planned (Albers and Lakens, 2018). The variance components are the part of a pilot worth carrying over. The effect is better set to a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI), the smallest effect of theoretical or practical importance. For an effect keyed cond, as in the crossed_mixed_rt example, pass sesoi = c(cond = 0.03), or set spec$fixed$coefficients$cond <- 0.03 on the returned specification. Every call reports in a message which coefficients it took from the fit, with their values.

When no SESOI can be argued for, effects = "safeguard" takes safeguard values (Perugini, Gallucci and Costantini, 2014). Each coefficient not named in sesoi becomes the bound of its two-sided safeguard_level interval nearer zero, by default that of the 60% interval. The interval is the estimate plus or minus a quantile times the standard error from vcov(fit). For an lme4 fit, the quantile is normal, qnorm((1 + safeguard_level) / 2), which is 0.84 at the default. The normal quantile treats the standard error as known, so the interval is too narrow when the subjects or items are few. For a lmerTest fit, the quantile is a t quantile on the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom that lmerTest reports, which allow for the uncertainty in the variance components, although only approximately. When lmerTest cannot give them for every coefficient, all coefficients take the normal quantile, and the message names the distribution used. An interval that includes zero stops the call with an error naming the effect. The pilot then leaves even the sign of the effect open, and a value of zero would plan a study of no effect at all. Such an effect needs a value in sesoi. By default, the conditions that design_conditions() builds for sweep_spec() include one with every named effect at zero, which shows how often a design declares an effect that is not there.

Whatever their source, the coefficients of the specification are the effects its data are simulated with. A named numeric focal in power_mixed() changes only the true values against which Type S and Type M are computed. The simulated effect stays as it was, so powering a study for another effect means changing the specification.

Every number is taken on the scale the model was fitted on, and the returned family is Gaussian by default, because that is what a lmer fit is. A model of log reaction times therefore yields an intercept, coefficients and residual standard deviation on the log scale, which is the right thing for the lognormal and shifted_lognormal families, whose linear predictor lives on that scale as well. Ask for one of those with family, in the list form when the family needs a parameter the fit cannot supply, as in family = list(family = "shifted_lognormal", shift = 200).

Whether a numeric column of the model frame was a contrast-coded factor or a continuous covariate is not recorded anywhere in a fitted model, so it is inferred here. A column that is a factor, a character vector or a logical vector is treated as categorical and its own contrast coding is read with stats::contrasts(), which makes the emitted contrast-column names agree with the coefficient names lme4 produced. A numeric column with exactly two distinct values is also treated as categorical, on the reasoning that a two-valued numeric predictor in a factorial experiment is a coded factor far more often than it is a covariate. Any other numeric column becomes a continuous predictor, with mean and sd taken from the data, one value per unit for a unit-level variable so that an unbalanced design does not distort them. This is a heuristic and nothing more, it is reported by a message on every call, and a genuine two-valued covariate has to be moved from factors to predictors by hand.

A column is placed as between a unit when it holds one value within every member of that unit, and as vary_within when it takes several values inside every unit; the same test gives a continuous predictor its varies_by, which becomes "observation" when the predictor varies inside every unit. A model that codes one factor twice, once as a factor for its fixed effect and once as a numeric contrast for a random slope, gives two separate specification terms, because the two columns are separate columns in the model frame and nothing in the fit ties them together.

Two or more factors placed between the same unit become one factor whose levels are their cells, and a message says so. The first-listed factor varies slowest, and each label joins the components' labels with ".". Two between factors over one unit need specification version 0.4, which allocates them jointly. Up to version 0.3, each was assigned to blocks of its unit on its own, which confounded their effects, and validate_spec() refuses them in a specification declaring an earlier version. The factor of cells allocates the units as version 0.4 allocates the separate factors, and every release that reads version 0.3 reads it, so the returned specification declares 0.3. The combined factor carries every component's contrast columns under the names the fit gave them, so each coefficient the fit estimated, interactions included, still names a column. Every cell then receives units, in equal numbers whenever the number of units is a multiple of the number of cells.

Interactions need one further step. lme4 writes the interaction of two model-frame columns as a:b, which is already the specification's convention, but model_data() gives an interaction its own product column named a_b, so a specification built from a fit of pilotr's own modelling data would otherwise acquire a spurious independent term. Such a column is recognised by checking the product identity in the data, which both avoids mistaking a column called z_freq for an interaction and settles where to split a name with several underscores. A recognised product column is reported and re-keyed to a:b, and it contributes no factor or predictor of its own.

Grouping factors named subject and item are used as they stand. Otherwise the one with the most levels becomes subject, the largest remaining factor that is crossed with it becomes item, and every other grouping factor becomes an extra random entry with the over and n fields that pilotr's additional grouping factors take, over being decided by which unit the factor partitions. Any renaming is reported by a message and recorded in the group_mapping attribute of the result. When each subject saw only some of the items, the item unit gains a per_subject count, so that the recovered design keeps the partial crossing of the original.

A factor that varies within both units is crossed with every subject-item pair unless it sets counterbalance, a field of specification version 0.4. A pilot run in counterbalanced lists, as priming studies usually are, showed each subject each item at one level only. The levels rotated across lists of subjects, so that every item appeared at each level. When every subject-item pair of the pilot holds one level of a factor, and every subject and every item holds two or more, the returned specification sets counterbalance to TRUE on that factor and declares version 0.4. Each subject then meets each item at one level, the levels rotating over subjects and items as described under Counterbalanced lists in the specification (spec/SPEC.md). The simulated data name each subject's list in a column list. Factors rotated together, as two two-level factors over four lists, are all counterbalanced, and a message names them. Releases that read no version above 0.3 refuse such a specification.

counterbalance = FALSE returns the crossed specification of earlier versions, which those releases read, with a warning. It has twice the pilot's observations per subject for a two-level factor, three times for a three-level one and four times for two two-level factors rotated together. The power computed from it is therefore too high. Take the variance components of the crossed_mixed_rt example, with 30 subjects, 24 items and an effect of 0.05 on the log scale. By the formulas of Judd, Westfall and Kenny (2017), power is then about 0.80 for the crossed design and 0.55 for the counterbalanced one. The counterbalanced study needs about 1.8 times the subjects to match the crossed one. A release that reads no version above 0.3 takes a two-level design written with a list factor between subjects and an item-set factor between items, as in the two-list example among the worked encodings of the specification. The crossed specification and the warning also come back, whatever counterbalance says, when each subject of the pilot saw only some of the items. The specification then keeps per_subject, which version 0.4 does not combine with counterbalance, since that field needs every subject to see every item. They come back as well when the pilot's model has a column or grouping factor named list, as a model that fits the list beside the condition does. Version 0.4 gives that name to the column holding each subject's list, and no other column may share it. The warning then asks for the term to be renamed in the pilot's data and the model refitted.

Alternatively, keep the crossed specification and drop the rows that a counterbalanced study would not observe, through the prep argument of power_mixed() and precision_design(). That function receives each simulated data set and returns the modelling data, so it ends by calling model_data(). With workers > 1 it runs in worker processes that have not attached pilotr and cannot see the caller's variables, so it has to call pilotr::model_data() and carry the specification with it. A function made by another function carries it once that function has forced its argument, as in this rotation over two lists for the crossed_mixed_rt example, whose factor is condition:

counterbalance <- function(spec) {
  force(spec)
  function(d) {
    level <- match(d$condition, spec$factors[[1]]$levels) - 1L
    pilotr::model_data(spec, d[(d$subject %% 2L + d$item + level) %% 2L == 0L, ])
  }
}
power_mixed(spec, prep = counterbalance(spec), workers = 4)

A boundary-singular pilot fit is carried across as it stands, which means a variance estimated at zero or a correlation estimated at exactly plus or minus one. Those are faithful readings of the fit, and no kind of defect, but they are also the sign that the random-effect structure was richer than the pilot could support, and a power analysis resting on them will inherit that (Bates et al., 2015). Widening the design, or simplifying the structure before refitting, is the remedy.

References

Albers, C. and Lakens, D. (2018). When power analyses based on pilot data are biased: Inaccurate effect size estimators and follow-up bias. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 74, 187-195. doi:10.1016/j.jesp.2017.09.004

Bates, D., Kliegl, R., Vasishth, S. and Baayen, H. (2015). Parsimonious mixed models. arXiv. doi:10.48550/arXiv.1506.04967

DeBruine, L. M. and Barr, D. J. (2021). Understanding mixed-effects models through data simulation. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 4(1). doi:10.1177/2515245920965119

Green, P. and MacLeod, C. J. (2016). SIMR: an R package for power analysis of generalized linear mixed models by simulation. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 7(4), 493-498. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.12504

Judd, C. M., Westfall, J. and Kenny, D. A. (2017). Experiments with more than one random factor: Designs, analytic models, and statistical power. Annual Review of Psychology, 68, 601-625. doi:10.1146/annurev-psych-122414-033702

Kumle, L., Vo, M. L.-H. and Draschkow, D. (2021). Estimating power in (generalized) linear mixed models: An open introduction and tutorial in R. Behavior Research Methods, 53, 2528-2543. doi:10.3758/s13428-021-01546-0

Perugini, M., Gallucci, M. and Costantini, G. (2014). Safeguard power as a protection against imprecise power estimates. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 9(3), 319-332. doi:10.1177/1745691614528519

See also

simulate_design() to simulate from the recovered specification, power_mixed() to run the power analysis it was read off the fit for, and model_formula() for the analysis model a specification implies.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # Stand in for a pilot study: simulate a small design and fit it.
  pilot <- build_spec(list(name = "pilot", seed = 1, design_kind = "within",
    include_items = TRUE, n_subject = 30, n_item = 20, factor_name = "cond",
    lev1 = "a", lev2 = "b", intercept = 6, effect = 0.05,
    subj_int_sd = 0.12, subj_slope_sd = 0, subj_corr = 0,
    item_int_sd = 0.08, item_slope_sd = 0, item_corr = 0,
    family = "shifted_lognormal", resp_name = "", sigma = 0.3, shift = 200))
  fit <- lme4::lmer(model_formula(pilot), data = model_data(pilot, simulate_design(pilot)))

  # Read the design back off the fit, scaled up to the sample size being planned.
  spec <- spec_from_model(fit, n_subject = 60, n_item = 40)
  spec$random$subject$intercept_sd
  attr(spec, "column_kinds")
  head(simulate_design(spec))

  # The effect is the pilot's estimate. Plan for a smallest effect size of interest, here 0.03
  # on the log scale, or for the bound of the estimate's 60% interval nearer zero.
  spec_from_model(fit, n_subject = 60, n_item = 40, sesoi = c(effect = 0.03))$fixed
  spec_from_model(fit, n_subject = 60, n_item = 40, effects = "safeguard")$fixed
}
#> spec_from_model() read 'effect' as categorical factor. A fitted model does not record which of its numeric columns were coded factors, so please check that reading.
#> spec_from_model() took 'effect' = 0.0669 from the fit, as the pilot estimated it. A pilot's estimates are noisy, and a study powered for them tends to be underpowered. Set a smallest effect size of interest with `sesoi`, or use effects = "safeguard" (see ?spec_from_model).
